title: Rein Raises $25M Series A to Secure the Agent Economy
text: We raised $25M to help enterprises deploy AI agents safely with runtime visibility, behavioral governance and real-time protection. Rein Raises $25M Series A to Secure the Agent Economy Skip to content $25M SERIES A $35M in total funding to date Read Now × Menu Menu Platform Solutions Finance Agent Security Healthcare Agent Security SaaS & Retail Agent Security Post Mythos Readiness Blog Newsroom About See the Magic Home / Blog / We Raised A $25M Series A to Secure the Agent Economy Article We Raised A $25M Series A to Secure the Agent Economy We're announcing a $25 million Series A, bringing our total funding to $35 million. Here's why. Matan Bar-Efrat | 08.10.26 | 4 min Key Takeaways The agent economy has arrived. According to IDC, 95% of companies now run AI agents in production, handling real customers, data and money. Gartner projects the market for securing AI will reach nearly $4.8 billion in 2027 and nearly $7.7 billion by 2028. Security teams face two problems at once. They have to deploy their own agents safely and defend against AI-powered attacks that move at machine speed, faster than a human team can triage or patch. The biggest risks sit in agent behavior. Hidden prompt injections, customer-facing agents that can be manipulated and trust passed between agents all show up at runtime. Code scans, posture dashboards and gateway logs miss them. Runtime is where agents have to be secured. Rein sees every agent action, holds each agent to its role and blocks harmful actions before they execute. It does this without routing data through a gateway or proxy. Rein's momentum backs the thesis. Since the January 2026 launch, revenue has grown 8x and customers 5x. The new $25M Series A, which brings total funding to $35M, will go into product, Agent Breakers research and hiring. The Agent Economy Is Already Here Today we’re announcing a $25 million Series A, bringing our total funding to $35 million. Since our January 2026 launch, we’ve seen 8x revenue growth and 5x more customers. But this post isn’t (just) about the round. It’s about why the round matters: the agent economy is arriving faster than anyone planned for, and it can’t scale without a security layer built for it. The shift is no longer theoretical. According to IDC, 95% of companies now have AI agents deployed in production. Not in pilots or sandboxes, but in production, touching real customers, real data and real money. In addition, according to Gartner , the market for securing AI is projected to reach nearly $4.8 billion in 2027, up 68.7% from 2026, and nearly $7.7 billion by 2028. The reason is simple. The promise of the agent economy rests on one idea: that companies can replace entire workflows with AI and capture substantial economic value by doing so. Onboarding, claims processing, customer support, procurement, research and code review are all being handed to agents that act on their own, around the clock, at a scale no team of people could match. That value is only real if enterprises can trust what their agents do. Every workflow an agent takes over is a workflow that now runs without a human watching each step. Making that safe is what Rein exists to do. We don’t see ourselves as a brake on the agent economy. We see ourselves as what makes it possible. https://reinsec.io/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Series-polished-longer.mp4 Two AI Agent Security Problems, Arriving at the Same Time In conversations with CISOs across financial services, healthcare, SaaS, retail and energy, we keep hearing about the same two challenges. They are different problems, but they are landing on security teams at once. Deploying agents safely. The agents enterprises build are given broad access to business systems, data and workflows. They read documents, call APIs, move records and trigger downstream actions automatically. More and more often, they act on instructions passed along by another system or another agent, not by a person. Security teams need to know what every agent is doing, govern what it’s allowed to do, and stop a harmful action before it executes, not after the incident review. Defending against adversarial AI. The same technology is now in attackers’ hands. AI-driven attacks probe, adapt and exploit at machine speed, far faster than a human team can triage alerts or ship a patch. When the attacker moves in seconds, the old sequence of detect, investigate, then fix breaks down. The model has to flip: block first, remediate afterwards. Most security tools were built for one of these worlds, or for neither. Enterprises need both covered, in one place, at runtime. AI Agent Security Risks Traditional Tools Can’t See Here’s what surprises most security leaders: the biggest agent risks are invisible to the tools they already own. They don’t show up in a code scan, a posture dashboard or a gateway log. They live in the actions agents take at runtime, often several steps removed from anything a person asked for. These are the risks we find every week: The PDF that wasn’t just a PDF. A global enterprise’s onboarding agent opened what looked like an ordinary document. Hidden inside was a prompt injection instructing the agent to act outside its intended role. Nothing about the file looked malicious to a person or a traditional scanner. Rein detected the out-of-role action and blocked it before any damage was done. The shopping assistant that could be turned. At Black Hat USA 2026 , our research team, Agent Breakers, showed how we compromised the AI shopping agent of a major U.S. retailer. The agent was live, customer-facing and built by a sophisticated team. It still had a path to abuse that no existing control had flagged. Instructions from a machine, not a human. When one agent hands a task to another, the second agent often inherits trust it was never meant to have. title: Security for the Post-Mythos AI Era
text: Prepare for the post-Mythos era with Rein. Block zero-days and exploitable CVEs at runtime, prioritize real risks, and protect AI agents at machine speed. Security for the Post-Mythos AI Era Skip to content $25M SERIES A $35M in total funding to date Read Now × Menu Menu Platform Solutions Finance Agent Security Healthcare Agent Security SaaS & Retail Agent Security Post Mythos Readiness Blog Newsroom About See the Magic Get Ready for the Vuln-Pocalypse Frontier models can now discover and exploit both zero-days and known CVEs at machine speed. Rein stops them at runtime, then helps your team remediate only what is actually exploitable. The optimal defense for the post-Mythos era. Book a Demo THE NEW REALITY The Vuln-Pocalypse is Here Mythos and other frontier models created two different problems for security teams, at the same time. The Zero Day Flood AI finds zero-days in your apps, agents and their dependencies, then writes the exploit. There's no CVE and no patch. If the target is an agent with API keys and code execution, a breach can follow in seconds. The Vulnerability Flood The same models, when used internally, flood your team with thousands of new vulnerabilities, far more than anyone can patch. Rein flags the ones that are actually exploitable and blocks attacks on them until you fix them. Time to Exploit Dropped from Years to Hours The Rein Way Prevent. buy time. fix. Rein watches every action your agents and apps take in production, detects and blocks anything that deviates, and filters your vulnerability flood down to what's actually exploitable. Both problems, solved. Book a Demo Rein shows us what’s really happening in our agents and apps, so we can detect and stop actual exploitation attempts, understand what the application is actually doing, and support developers with the visibility they need, all without impacting production. — Jonathan Jaffe, CISO, Lemonade Security Built for Enterprise Agents Protect Enterprise Agents at Machine Speed Mythos can hit your agents, frameworks, the tools they call, their dependencies, and apps. Rein protects and prevents attacks on your most critical agents with one read-only sidecar. Enterprise Agent AI security Uncover every agent, tool, framework, prompt, and action in production. Agent Detection & Response Zero-days and one-days, blocked at runtime. MCP Security Uncover what your Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers actually do at runtime. Supply Chain Security See which vulnerable functions actually run, which CVE is exploitable. Code Security See which findings are executable and which aren't See the Platform You Probably Have Some Questions. Can AI find and exploit vulnerabilities on its own? Increasingly, yes. A new class of AI can discover a previously undocumented flaw and write a working exploit for it at machine speed, with no CVE to warn you first. Against an AI agent that holds API keys and can run code, the gap from discovery to breach can close in seconds, which is why CVE patching can't keep up. This is the post-Mythos reality, and it's what Rein is built for: it detects any agent action that deviates from a learned baseline, so the exploit is stopped whether or not anyone has seen it before. How can Rein stop a zero-day that has no CVE and no patch? It doesn't look for the exploit, it looks for the behavior. Rein learns how each agent and app normally behaves in your production and detects any action that deviates, at the moment of execution. A novel zero-day, a one-day, a prompt injection, and a misconfiguration all look the same to Rein: an agent doing something it isn't supposed to. A Mythos-class scanner flooded our backlog. How does Rein decide what's actually exploitable? It checks three things scanners can't: whether the vulnerable code is actually loaded in production, whether it's reachable in your application logic, and whether it's running in production. What survives all three is the short list that matters. Does Rein run in production, and what does it cost us? Yes. Rein deploys as one read-only sidecar that runs alongside your agents in production and is built to stay out of their way. In production it adds under half a millisecond of latency per request, keeps CPU overhead under 1%, and uses around 20 MB of memory, with no measurable impact on uptime. It ships structural metadata, not full payloads, so there is nothing heavy in the request path. Does our code or execution data leave our environment? No. Rein uses a fully in-org data model. All data stays inside your environment, so data privacy and compliance is not compromised or requires additional audit. Does Rein replace our SAST/SCA scanners, or work alongside them? Both, over time. Day one, Rein tells you which existing findings are real and blocks what your scanners miss. As that production truth proves out, most teams lean on the noisy tools far less. What is reachability analysis, and how is it different from a vulnerability scan? A vulnerability scan tells you which libraries contain known flaws. Reachability analysis tells you which of those flaws an attacker can actually reach and execute in your environment. Scanning tells you what's vulnerable; execution context tells you what's exploitable. Rein maps the exact vulnerable function to what's running in production, so a flaw only counts when an attacker can reach it and it actually runs. That pinpoints the specific exploitable library instead of the whole package, and a backlog of hundreds of CVEs collapses to the handful that are real. title: Why We Started Rein Security: AppSec Without Guesswork
text:
Why We Started Rein Security: AppSec Without Guesswork. Why We Started Rein Security: AppSec Without Guesswork

# Why We Started Rein Security

Matan Bar-Efrat, Co-founder and CEO at Rein breaks down why AppSec has been operating through approximations- and why Rein started by going after execution reality instead.

Matan Bar-Efrat

25.01.26

## The Beginning

Like any good story, this one started with a run in the park.

After weeks of ideation trying to find the right problem, it suddenly clicked. I got home, called Netanel, and asked:

> How come, in 2024, it’s still so easy to hack web applications?

That question became an obsession. We spent months asking “why.” Why is the AppSec market so fragmented? Why does it feel like a wedge between security and dev? And why, despite massive budgets and real effort, does AppSec still produce so much noise and so little control?

## We validated this with 100+ CISOs

We took our thesis to the field. Over 100 conversations with CISOs and security leaders. The complaints were predictable: too noisy, too many false positives, low signal, siloed tools.

But what stuck with me wasn’t the frustration. It was something a CISO at a large fintech told us: “I’ve accepted that we’ll never truly know what’s happening inside our apps. We just manage the uncertainty.”

That resignation – the idea that AppSec is fundamentally about educated guessing – is what made us stubborn.

Matan Bar Efrat, Co-founder & CEO, Rein and Netanel Rubin, Co-founder & CTO, Rein

Rein Raises $25M Series A to Secure the Agent Economy. Rein Raises $25M Series A to Secure the Agent Economy

# We Raised A $25M Series A to Secure the Agent Economy

We're announcing a $25 million Series A, bringing our total funding to $35 million. Here's why.

Matan Bar-Efrat

08.10.26

### Key Takeaways

- The agent economy has arrived. According to IDC, 95% of companies now run AI agents in production, handling real customers, data and money. Gartner projects the market for securing AI will reach nearly $4.8 billion in 2027 and nearly $7.7 billion by 2028.
- Security teams face two problems at once. They have to deploy their own agents safely and defend against AI-powered attacks that move at machine speed, faster than a human team can triage or patch.
- The biggest risks sit in agent behavior. Hidden prompt injections, customer-facing agents that can be manipulated and trust passed between agents all show up at runtime. Code scans, posture dashboards and gateway logs miss them.
- Runtime is where agents have to be secured. Rein sees every agent action, holds each agent to its role and blocks harmful actions before they execute. It does this without routing data through a gateway or proxy.
- Rein's momentum backs the thesis. Since the January 2026 launch, revenue has grown 8x and customers 5x. The new $25M Series A, which brings total funding to $35M, will go into product, Agent Breakers research and hiring.

title: Rein Launches the First Security Platform for Enterprise Agents
text:
Rein Launches the First Security Platform for Enterprise Agents. Rein Launches First Enterprise AI Agent Security Platform

# We're Launching the First Security Platform Designed for Enterprise Agents

Agents Grew Up. It's Time Their Security Did Too.. Today, we're launching the first security platform purpose-built for Enterprise Agents.

Shlomi Ashkenazy

15.06.26

### Key Takeaways

- "Agents" means two different things. Weekend hacks and productivity tools are not the same as production agents processing payments, underwriting insurance, or touching customer data. Conflating them is the core security mistake.
- Enterprise Agents are a new category. Built by teams, running at scale, on regulated infrastructure, with decisions that are auditable and customer-facing. They demand security built specifically for them - not retrofitted from Era 1 or 2 tools.
- Existing solutions were designed for the wrong world. Gateway-level alerts, static rules, and network-layer visibility don't give you the execution chain you need when a prompt injection can trigger a real transaction.
- Routing sensitive agentic data through a vendor isn't security - it's liability. Full observability with data sovereignty shouldn't be a trade-off.
- Rein is purpose-built for Era 3. Four pillars - Discovery, Coverage, Guardrails, Privacy - delivered via an in-org sidecar that sees the full execution chain without ever transmitting your data externally.

There’s a word that’s been everywhere for the past two years: agents.

Executives talk about agents. VCs fund agents

# From chatbot to RCE: hacking a retailer's AI shopping assistant

A grocery chatbot, reachable from the public mobile app, was talked into leaking its hidden instructions and then into running attacker code on a top-3 US retailer's servers. Netanel Rubin led the team that did it.

Netanel Rubin

Co-Founder & CTO / Rein Security

He got into AppSec at 16 as a pentester for Israeli national banks. After serving in the Israeli Intelligence Corps he joined Check Point, where he found more than a dozen zero-days, mostly unauthenticated RCEs, in the software running much of the internet at the time: Wikipedia, WordPress, Bugzilla, Magento and vBulletin among them. He has presented at DEF CON, Black Hat and CCC. He later founded the security consultancy Holcy, acquired by Lab42 where he became CTO, and now co-founds Rein Security. At Black Hat USA 2026 he and Dan Avraham presented "Bye Bye AI" on chaining flaws in a top-3 US retailer's AI shopping assistant all the way to remote code execution.

# Everyone Was Wrong About Agentic AI and Application Security

Netanel Rubin, Co-founder and CTO at Rein gives us a first-principles takedown of 25 years of AppSec guesswork- and the story of how real runtime context finally breaks the attacker–defender stalemate.

Netanel Rubin

25.01.26

### Key Takeaways

- Traditional AppSec tools cannot uncover enterprise-agent reality. SAST, SCA, and API security tools lack visibility into enterprise-agent execution flows and runtime behaviour.
- Full execution tracing reveals real exploitability. Visibility into API calls, resource access, and execution flows exposes real business risk instead of theoretical vulnerabilities.
- Gateway, proxy, and eBPF approaches miss the execution context. These architectures cannot deliver complete in-process visibility into enterprise-agent behaviour.

## How It All Started

A year ago, my co-founder Matan called me with a question that should have been easy to answer.

“How is it still so easy to hack modern web applications in 2024?”

I didn’t have a good answer.

I’d spent most of my career on the offensive side of application security – pentester, vulnerability researcher, eventually CTO. My job was simple and endlessly fascinating: breaking into systems no one had broken into before. I was good at it. And if you’d asked me why attackers always seemed to have the upper hand, I would have given you the standard explanation: asymmetric
